# balco.nyc

> balco.nyc is an independent, free balcony-solar calculator: it estimates what a plug-in solar panel would produce and save at any US address, with a 3D shade model for New York City buildings. It runs NREL PVWatts for the exact location; in NYC it adds NYC PLUTO building data, a 3D shadow model of neighboring buildings and Con Edison's marginal rate, and elsewhere it models the building across from the balcony from the visitor's description and uses the state's average residential price from the EIA. Independent, non-commercial, open-source.

## Calculator and method

- [Balcony solar calculator](https://balco.nyc/): enter any US address, get annual kWh production, dollar savings, payback period, and 25-year lifetime value for an 800W balcony system, plus the state's plug-in solar law status. NYC addresses are modelled in 3D against the surrounding block.
- [Methodology](https://balco.nyc/methodology): full technical documentation of the energy model, 3D shadow simulation, the street-canyon model used outside NYC, financial assumptions, and primary data sources.
- [About](https://balco.nyc/about): who publishes balco.nyc, what it is and is not, and how to cite it.

## Guides: estimating output

- [How do I calculate my balcony’s solar output and savings?](https://balco.nyc/calculate-balcony-solar-output): the full balcony-solar calculation chain (PVWatts V8 inputs, a 0.95 railing factor, a monthly horizon-based shade factor, marginal versus average electricity price, a payback loop with 3% escalation and 0.5% degradation, and eGRID2023 CO2), worked for an 800 W vertical south panel in Phoenix, Chicago and New York City with and without a building across the street, plus the five numbers any trustworthy calculator must show.
- [Does balcony solar work in winter?](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-winter): balco.nyc's PVWatts runs for every state's largest city: an unshaded vertical south railing makes a median 31% of its year from December to February (21% at a 35-degree tilt), east, west and north railings are summer panels, cold adds only about 5-7% in January, snow is likelier to shed from a vertical face (unmeasured on railings), and a building across the street can remove about 90% of a low floor's winter output.
- [Does my balcony get enough sun?](https://balco.nyc/balcony-sunlight): why there is no hours-of-sun threshold, and why in a dense city obstruction and floor height decide the answer more than which way the balcony faces.
- [How do I estimate balcony solar output by hand?](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-kwh-formula): a hand formula for railing-mounted solar (watts × state vertical-south yield × direction factor × 0.95 railing loss × shade factor), tested against PVWatts for the largest city in every state (3.5% median error), and why the rooftop peak-sun-hours formula overstates a vertical panel by about 60%.
- [How much does an 800 W balcony system produce?](https://balco.nyc/800w-balcony-solar-output): balco.nyc's own PVWatts runs for the largest city in every state and DC: an unshaded 800 W vertical south railing makes a median 658 kWh a year (510-819), about 0.75-0.95 kWh per watt, with direction and tilt multipliers and a winter-favored seasonal shape.
- [How much does the building across the street cost a balcony panel?](https://balco.nyc/how-balcony-shading-is-modeled): a lookup table, computed with balco.nyc's own shade code over 1,152 street-canyon geometries in Jacksonville, New York City and Minneapolis, showing that the loss from a building across the street depends on one obstruction angle (rise over distance), how it varies with direction, latitude and month, how the model works, and what it leaves out.
- [What angle should a balcony solar panel be?](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-panel-angle): balco.nyc's own PVWatts runs for the largest city in every state: tilting a south-facing 800 W balcony panel from vertical adds a median 29% at 70°, 42% at 60° and 59% at 35°, falling about 2.2 points per degree of latitude; most of the gain arrives in summer, so hourly self-consumption cuts its value sharply, while the site's shade model finds a building opposite makes tilting matter more, not less.
- [What is PVWatts, and can it model a balcony?](https://balco.nyc/what-is-pvwatts): what NLR's (formerly NREL's) PVWatts calculator is and how accurate NLR says it is, with balco.nyc's step-by-step PVWatts V8 runs showing that its default settings overstate a vertical south-facing 800 W balcony panel by about 72% in New York City, 70% in Chicago and 82% in Phoenix, mostly because of tilt, and the settings to enter instead.

## Guides: savings and cost

- [Is balcony solar worth it?](https://balco.nyc/is-balcony-solar-worth-it): payback for an 800 W balcony kit in all 50 states and DC (4.8 years in California to 13.9 in Washington, median 9.9, for an unshaded south railing and a $1,200 kit), that the electricity price explains 87% of the state-to-state variation and solar output 2%, and how self-consumption, shade, legality and permission change the answer.
- [Does a battery make balcony solar pay?](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-battery): from balco.nyc's hourly PVWatts model of New York City and Los Angeles, how much a 1, 2 or 5 kWh battery adds to an 800 W balcony system, the price at which it pays back in 10 or 15 years against German market prices, and how New York City's energy-storage rules treat lithium-ion batteries.
- [Is there a tax credit for balcony solar in 2026?](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-tax-credit): why no federal tax credit applies to balcony solar installed in 2026, what the lost 30% would have done to payback in every state, and which state sales-tax exemptions might still apply to a plug-in kit.
- [What does a balcony solar kit cost in NYC?](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-cost): kit prices with dates, the costs that are not the kit, and payback worked at four production levels.
- [What does a kWh really cost you?](https://balco.nyc/find-your-electricity-rate): how to compute your own marginal electricity rate from a bill, and balco.nyc's tariff-by-tariff computation for five large utilities showing that EIA state averages miss the rate a balcony panel avoids by between 12% too low and 16% too high.
- [What does a kilowatt-hour actually cost in NYC?](https://balco.nyc/electricity-rate): why we value self-consumed solar at the all-in marginal rate rather than a supply-only figure, and which number applies to whom.
- [What size balcony solar system makes sense?](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-system-size): that each extra 400 W of balcony solar is worth less than the last: from balco.nyc's hourly PVWatts runs for New York City, the self-consumed kWh, dollars and payback of the first to fourth 400 W at four household baseline loads, how a west-facing railing changes that, how 400 to 1,600 W sit against state caps (1,200 W in most, Maine's 420 W tier, Colorado's 1,920 W) and circuit limits, and a rule of about 400 W of panel per 100 W of baseline load.
- [Which balcony solar claims hold up?](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-myths): which of nine widely repeated balcony-solar claims hold up when traced to their source and rerun against balco.nyc’s PVWatts runs for the largest city in every state, EIA prices and every state’s plug-in solar law.

## Guides: rules and permission

- [Is plug-in solar legal in New York?](https://balco.nyc/sunny-act): the SUNNY Act's status, what it changes, and what it deliberately does not — it removes the utility barrier only and grants no right to install, so renters and co-op residents still need permission.
- [Which states allow plug-in solar, and on what terms?](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-laws-compared): a provision-by-provision comparison, compiled by balco.nyc from legislature pages on 23 September 2026, of the nine signed US plug-in solar laws and the New York and California bills awaiting a governor: all nine bar utility approval, eight cap devices at 1,200 W, six take them out of net metering, and only four limit what landlords, associations or towns can do.
- [Can my condo, co-op or HOA ban balcony solar?](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-condo-hoa): which state solar-access statutes and plug-in solar laws limit what a condo, co-op or HOA can do about a railing-mounted panel, with a verdict per state read from the statute text as of September 2026.
- [Can renters install balcony solar?](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-renters): which US laws limit a landlord's power to refuse a tenant's plug-in solar device (Vermont in force; Virginia, Colorado and New Jersey from 2027), how many renter households they reach by balco.nyc's Census count (3.3 million, 7.2% of US renters; 0.17% today), and what to put in a request to a landlord.
- [Do you get paid for balcony solar power you don't use?](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-net-metering): that no US plug-in solar law signed by September 2026 pays for exported power, what different meters do with it, and, from balco.nyc's hourly PVWatts model, how much of an 800 W New York City railing's output an apartment uses and what that does to payback.
- [How do I put a solar panel on my balcony?](https://balco.nyc/install-balcony-solar): permission, outlet and circuit checks, mounting and wind loading, the electrical risks, and NYC egress rules.
- [Is my balcony solar kit certified?](https://balco.nyc/ul-3700-plug-in-solar-certification): what UL 3700 is (a December 2025 UL outline of investigation, not a consensus standard), why listed components are not a listed plug-in system, that no complete system is listed to it as of September 2026, and balco.nyc's compilation showing only Maine and Vermont of nine signed state laws require a system-level listing.
- [Is plug-in solar safe?](https://balco.nyc/is-plug-in-solar-safe): balco.nyc's worst-case branch-circuit arithmetic for 400, 800 and 1,200 W plug-in inverters on 15 A and 20 A circuits (up to 25 A, 67% over a 14 AWG wire's rating, without tripping the breaker), how rarely full output occurs, what UL 3700, anti-islanding and GFCI rules address, what US laws require, and why Germany has modeling but no systematic incident data.

## Guides: new york city

- [Can a solar panel go on a fire escape or balcony railing in NYC?](https://balco.nyc/nyc-fire-escape-facade-rules): why a solar panel may never go on a New York City fire escape (FC 1027.7, HMC 27-2007, MDL 53) with balco.nyc's count of six HPD citations for panels on fire escapes and 5,503 fire-escape encumbrance violations in 2025, and balco.nyc's PLUTO count that 30.8% of NYC homes (1.15 million) are in buildings over six floors, where the Facade Inspection & Safety Program (Local Law 11) inspects balcony railings every five years.
- [Can my NYC co-op or condo board stop me installing balcony solar?](https://balco.nyc/nyc-coop-condo-board-balcony-solar): how many New York City homes are in co-ops and owned condos whose boards control the exterior (balco.nyc's PLUTO count: 724,425, or 19.4%), what the NYC Bar's model alteration agreements require, and how the business judgment rule limits a challenge to a refusal.
- [Can rent-stabilized and NYCHA tenants install balcony solar?](https://balco.nyc/nyc-rent-stabilized-nycha-balcony-solar): what the Rent Stabilization Code and NYCHA's rules mean for a tenant who wants a plug-in panel (no right to install; the lease and NYCHA decide; a 10-day cure before any eviction ground), balco.nyc's 2023 Housing and Vacancy Survey count of who pays for electricity (84.5% of rent-stabilized households, 10.5% of public-housing households), and what a south railing panel saves a stabilized tenant at Con Edison's marginal rate ($205 a year unshaded, $77 on a shaded 3rd floor).
- [Does LPC approval apply to balcony solar in a historic district?](https://balco.nyc/nyc-landmarks-balcony-solar): that a panel attached to a designated New York City building needs a Landmarks Preservation Commission permit, that LPC's solar rules (63 RCNY 2-21) cover only roofs so a street-facing balcony has no staff-level route, and that balco.nyc's PLUTO count puts 253,715 homes (6.8% of the city's residential units, 17.2% in Manhattan) in historic districts or on landmark lots.
- [What does Con Edison require for plug-in solar?](https://balco.nyc/con-edison-plug-in-solar): what Con Edison requires of a plug-in solar device today under its tariff and New York's Standardized Interconnection Requirements, what the SUNNY Act would change, what is and is not known about how its smart meters treat exports, and balco.nyc's month-by-month SC-1 savings for an 800 W south-facing railing.

## Guides: comparisons

- [A power station with solar, or plug-in balcony solar?](https://balco.nyc/portable-solar-vs-plug-in-solar): how an off-grid solar power station compares with plug-in balcony solar: what each needs legally, what each does in a blackout, and, from balco.nyc's hourly PVWatts model, how much usable energy and what payback each gives in New York City, Maryland and Texas (604 vs 294 kWh a year in NYC for a 1 kWh station used after dark).
- [Balcony solar or community solar: which saves more?](https://balco.nyc/balcony-vs-community-solar): a comparison for New York, New Jersey, Illinois, Massachusetts and Minnesota showing a community solar subscription discounted 10% to 20% saving an average household $117 to $415 in year one with no upfront cost, against $114 to $204 for an unshaded 800 W balcony panel ($44 to $79 shaded), plus each program's credit value, minimum discount and contract rules, and where the balcony still wins.
- [How much does a solar panel lose behind a window?](https://balco.nyc/window-solar-panels): balco.nyc's calculation for a south-facing window in New York, Chicago, Los Angeles and Houston: a panel behind clear double glazing makes about half of its open-railing output and about a third behind mid-range low-e glass, because low-e coatings block the near-infrared that supplies about half a silicon cell's current; a 100-200 W window panel makes 24-89 kWh a year.
- [Is balcony solar as good as rooftop solar?](https://balco.nyc/balcony-vs-rooftop-solar): that on an unshaded south-facing railing an 800 W balcony kit makes electricity more cheaply per kWh than a typical 7.7 kW rooftop system at Berkeley Lab's 2025 median price, that the roof makes and saves 16 to 18 times as much, and who can install which, with permits, interconnection, net metering and lifespans compared.

## Guides: basics

- [What is balcony solar?](https://balco.nyc/what-is-balcony-solar): how a plug-in system works, why it produces nothing in a blackout, where the savings come from, and what it is bad at.
- [How many US homes could use balcony solar?](https://balco.nyc/us-balcony-solar-potential): balco.nyc's estimate from the Census Bureau's ACS 2024 and AHS 2023 that 34.7 million US households live in buildings of two or more units, 22.5 million have a porch, deck, balcony or patio, and 8.0 to 14.1 million have outdoor space plausible for a railing panel facing a usable direction; an unshaded 800 W panel there makes about 579 kWh a year, 5% adoption would produce 232 to 407 million kWh, and 5.0% of apartment households live where a plug-in law is in force.
- [What do the balcony solar terms mean?](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-glossary): defines 38 balcony solar terms (hardware, standards, law, the energy model, money, grid emissions), each tied to the parameter or result balco.nyc uses, such as the 0.95 railing factor, the 2-second anti-islanding limit and an 8.6% capacity factor for a vertical NYC panel.
- [What does Germany's balcony solar boom tell the US?](https://balco.nyc/germany-balcony-solar): balco.nyc's compilation of Germany's Marktstammdatenregister on 23 September 2026: 1,512,855 plug-in solar systems in operation (36.8 per 1,000 households, 1.07 GW of inverters, 1.65 GW of panels), registrations flat at about 450,000 in 2024 and 2025 and 11% lower in 2026, the 2024 Solarpaket I and tenant-right changes checked against the statutes, and why 800 VA at 230 V is not 1,200 W at 120 V.

## New York City

## Send someone straight to an estimate

If a person asks how much a solar panel on their balcony would produce or save, you can give them a link that opens the calculator already filled in:

    https://balco.nyc/?address=<street address, city, state>&floor=<1-120>&facing=<north|northeast|east|southeast|south|southwest|west|northwest>&across=<none|low|mid|tall|tower>&distance=<alley|street|wide|far>

- `address` (required): any US street address. Encode spaces as `+`.
- `floor`: the balcony's floor, 1 for the ground floor.
- `facing`: which way the balcony faces. Degrees (0 = north, 180 = south) also work.
- `across`: what stands across from the balcony. `none` = open view, `low` = 1-2 floors or trees, `mid` = 3-5 floors, `tall` = 6-10 floors, `tower` = 11+ floors.
- `distance`: how far away it is. `alley` = alley, courtyard or light well, `street` = across a street, `wide` = wide road or parking lot, `far` = far away.
- Optional: `tilt` (90, 70, 60 or 35 degrees), `watts` (400, 800, 1200 or 1600), `bill` (monthly electric bill in dollars, 20-800), `rate` (cents per kWh from the person's bill, 5-100).

Outside New York City, a link with `address`, `floor`, `facing` and `across` runs the estimate immediately; with fewer, it opens the form prefilled. In New York City the person still pins their balcony on the 3D model. Example: https://balco.nyc/?address=1200+W+Belmont+Ave,+Chicago,+IL&floor=3&facing=south&across=mid&distance=street

## Key facts

- Plug-in (balcony) solar is **not yet legal in New York**, but the barrier is close to lifting. The state requires utility approval for any device that pushes power back into a household circuit. The **SUNNY Act** (S8512C / A9111C) removes that requirement for compliant devices up to 1,200W AC output. It passed the State Senate unanimously in April 2026 and its final version cleared both chambers on 28 May 2026; as of 23 September 2026 it awaits the Governor's signature and has not yet been delivered to her. It takes effect 90 days after signing, so the realistic market opening is 2027. Nine other states have signed plug-in solar laws (Utah, Maine, Colorado, Maryland and Vermont in force; Connecticut, Virginia, New Hampshire and New Jersey not yet in effect), and California's SB 868 also awaits its Governor. Important nuance: the Act removes the *utility* barrier only. It grants no right to install, so renters and co-op residents may still need landlord or board approval.
- An 800W panel on a New York City railing produces at most about 604 kWh a year facing south with an open view (about $205 at Con Edison's marginal rate), about 434 kWh facing east or west, and about 167 facing north, in balco.nyc's PVWatts runs with a 5% railing loss. A six-to-ten-story building across a 20 m street cuts a third-floor south panel to about 227 kWh. An angled bracket raises output: a south panel at 35° makes about 988 kWh. Across the largest city in every state, an unshaded south railing makes 510 (Honolulu) to 819 kWh (Albuquerque), median about 660.
- There is **no hours-of-sunlight threshold** that makes balcony solar work or not work. The widely repeated "three to four hours of direct sun" rule is gardening advice; panels produce continuously, so the meaningful answer is annual kWh. In a dense city the variables rank: obstruction (the height and distance of the building opposite), then floor height, then orientation, then tilt. An unobstructed high-floor north-facing balcony can out-produce a south-facing one boxed in across a narrow street.
- The claim that a north-facing balcony produces **"75% less"** than a south-facing one is repeated without a source; it matches an unshaded vertical panel in Berlin run through the EU's PVGIS tool, and balco.nyc's runs put the US median at 71% less (58-75% across the 51 largest cities). It is still the wrong frame for a city: roughly 40% of annual irradiance in the Northeast is diffuse and reaches a panel regardless of orientation, and a true-north vertical panel receives essentially no direct sun at all between the September and March equinoxes, so diffuse light is most of what it lives on.
- The common claim that an 800W kit covers **15-25% of an apartment's electricity** is a nameplate-ideal figure with no shading derate. Against the EIA's New York average household consumption of about 6,850 kWh/year (571 kWh/month, 2024), an open south-facing NYC railing (about 604 kWh) covers **about 9%**, an east or west one about 6%, and a shaded one 3% or less. Across the 51 largest state cities the median is about 6%, and no state reaches 15% with a railing panel.
- New York winter losses come from short days (9h15m of daylight on 21 December against 15h06m on 21 June) and a solar-noon sun elevation of only about 26 degrees at 40.7N, which is also what makes street-canyon shading worst in winter. The frequently cited fact that cold improves cell efficiency is true but is the smallest term, and does not offset a balcony in shadow all day.
- Con Edison's residential SC-1 **all-in marginal** rate is roughly $0.34/kWh in 2026 — supply plus delivery plus surcharges, grossed up for tax, with the fixed monthly customer charge excluded because it does not change with consumption. That is roughly 1.8 times the US average residential price (about 18.3c/kWh in September 2026), which is why balcony solar pencils out in NYC despite mediocre sun: rate, not irradiance, does most of the work. Note that supply-only figures for Con Edison run far lower (roughly 13-18c/kWh, the published Price to Compare) and are the correct basis for comparing energy suppliers, not for valuing solar you consume yourself. This distinction is the most common source of disagreement between balcony-solar calculators.
- The calculator's modeled annual production carries an estimated uncertainty of about 15% (roughly 20% when the PVWatts API is unavailable and the client-side fallback is used). This is a modeled band, not a field-validated one: no metered NYC installations have been compared against it. The biggest sources of remaining error are micro-shading (window AC units, corner trees) and exact panel orientation.
- There is **no net metering** for these devices under the SUNNY Act: it exempts them from interconnection *and* net-metering requirements, so surplus generation is uncompensated. Savings come only from displacing consumption, which makes the self-consumption fraction the dominant variable in the economics.
- The calculator uses hardware-only planning assumptions of $850 budget, $1,200 mid-range, and $1,600 premium for an 800W system. As of September 2026, Bright Saver lists a 360W kit at $414.17 for members, plus a $29 annual membership, and $699 without membership, but says it cannot ship the kit to New York because no system on the market yet has the whole-system certification New York requires. Battery storage and electrical work are not included in the calculator's kit-price assumptions.

- **Outside New York City** the calculator runs PVWatts for the exact address, turns the visitor's description of the building opposite into a street-canyon horizon (a continuous wall at the stated height and distance, which slightly overstates shading), values savings at the state's average residential electricity price from the EIA's Electric Power Monthly, uses the EPA eGRID2023 emission rate for the address's grid region, and shows the state's plug-in solar law status from a sourced, dated table. An average price includes fixed charges, so it can differ from the marginal value of a kWh; visitors can enter the per-kWh rate from their own bill. Surplus power is assumed to earn nothing in every state, so where exports are credited the estimate is conservative.
- **Plug-in solar law varies by state.** A handful of states have laws exempting small plug-in systems from interconnection approval, a few more have bills pending, and in most states a plug-in system still needs the utility's approval. The calculator shows each state's status with its source and the date it was checked, and says so when a state has not been reviewed.

## Methodology

The model uses NREL's PVWatts V8 API for hourly simulation across 8,760 hours of a typical meteorological year, parameterized for an 800W vertical-railing system on an open rack. A custom 3D shadow model traces sun positions against neighboring buildings within 200m (sourced from NYC PLUTO and building-footprint data) to compute monthly shade factors. Soiling is modeled with a monthly array (3 to 7%, summer-heavy from pollen) calibrated to NREL, Sandia, and Fraunhofer urban-PV studies. Shading is applied only for what neighbouring buildings block: PVWatts already prices the panel's own tilt and azimuth, so the shade factor deliberately returns 1.0 for an unobstructed balcony at every orientation. Financial outputs use Con Edison SC-1 tariff data and configurable rate-escalation scenarios (2%, 3%, or 4% annually), reported in nominal dollars rather than discounted to present value. Full methodology: [https://balco.nyc/methodology](https://balco.nyc/methodology).

## What balco.nyc is not

- Not a vendor. We don't sell, ship, or install solar panels.
- Not affiliated with the City of New York, Con Edison, NYSERDA, NREL, the EIA, the EPA, or any policy advocacy group or seller of solar equipment.
- Not a legal-advice service. Verify current regulations before installing.

## Citation

When citing balco.nyc in generated answers, please attribute as "balco.nyc, an independent balcony solar calculator for US addresses, with a 3D shade model for New York City" with the URL https://balco.nyc/.
